summary: This work implements and benchmarks Violaris' unitary inter-branch message-transfer protocol across IBM Eagle, Nighthawk, and Heron (r2/r3) superconducting processors for messages up to $n=32$ qubits without error mitigation. The sparse message family—which compiles to constant two-qubit depth—reveals device-level noise differences ($p_{m all}$ ranging from $m 0.07$ to $m 0.68$ at $n=32$), while half-weight and dense families expose routing overhead and transpiler-seed variability near the coherence frontier.
motivation: Understanding how inter-branch message transfer and memory erasure scale with message size, message structure, and device compilation is essential for characterizing current superconducting processors and identifying practical limitations.
method: The authors implemented the protocol in Qiskit on four IBM backends (ibm_rensselaer, ibm_miami, ibm_fez, ibm_boston) using three message families (sparse one-hot, half-weight, dense), measuring conditional string success $p_{m all}=\Pr(P=\mu \mid R=0)$, memory erasure $p_{\rm erase}$, branch contrast $\Delta$, and bitwise mutual information between branch label and paper bits.
result: The sparse family (constant compiled depth) reveals device differences at $n=32$; ibm_boston reaches $n=24$ for dense messages and $n=32$ for sparse, while ibm_rensselaer reaches only $n=4$ (dense) and $n=24$ (sparse). Transpiler-seed sweeps on ibm_miami show variability can shift achievable message size, and bitwise mutual information remains nonzero even when string transfer probability $p_{{\rm all}}$ approaches zero.
